analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage to $6.15 while creating new overtime exemptions and letting states keep the old $5.15 floor.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 282-143 on March 9, 2000, but its text was folded into another bill and the Congress ended without any minimum wage increase becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $5.15 an hour in three steps to $6.15 by April 2002, worth about $1.00 an hour to a full-time minimum-wage worker. It pays for that politically with a package of business-friendly offsets: new exemptions from minimum wage and overtime rules for certain computer professionals, sales employees, and funeral directors, and a provision letting any state replace the federal wage with its own law that keeps the floor at $5.15, which would erase the raise in that state. The House passed it, but the increase never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the minimum wage in states that do not opt out, who would earn up to $1.00 more per hour by 2002 — roughly $2,000 a year for full-time work. The technology, funeral services, and technical-sales industries also gain, because their workers lose minimum wage and overtime protections. State governments gain the power to set their own wage floor as low as $5.15.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers near minimum wage, plus exempted industries

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.48 an hour in the year starting April 1, 2000, then $5.81 and finally $6.15 by April 1, 2002.
The full $1.00 increase is worth roughly $2,080 a year to a full-time worker paid at the minimum wage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers bear the higher payroll, except in states that opt out at $5.15. The workers in the newly exempted categories — certain computer professionals, sales employees, and funeral directors — give up minimum wage and overtime protections. Workers in states that choose to keep $5.15 get no raise at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers and newly exempted workers

drawbacks.text: Sections 2, 3, and 4 strip minimum wage and overtime protections from computer professionals paid at least $27.63 an hour, certain sales employees, and licensed funeral directors and embalmers — moving some workers out of coverage even as the wage floor rises for everyone else.
Section 5 lets any state keep a minimum wage of just $5.15 and apply it to the same workers the federal law would cover, effectively letting states opt out of the increase entirely.
The raise is phased in over three years beginning a year after introduction, so the full increase does not arrive until April 2002.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage increase is real and would matter to millions of low-paid workers, but the bill's design steadily erodes it: a state opt-out that can freeze the old $5.15 rate, and exemptions that take pay protections away from defined groups of workers to soften opposition from their employers. A supporter of a wage increase has to acknowledge that this version raises the floor everywhere except where states choose not to, and lowers protections for some workers in the process.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 282-143, but under the debate rule its text was added to the end of a separate bill (H.R. 3081) and H.R. 3846 itself was laid on the table; the Senate never acted, the Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and no minimum wage increase became law — the federal rate stayed at $5.15 for years afterward.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 8, 2000, and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which never held a markup; instead the Rules Committee wrote a rule (H. Res. 434) bringing it straight to the floor packaged with H.R. 3081, with H.R. 3846's text to be added to that bill if passed.

Rep. Steve Largent raised a budget point of order that the bill imposed an unfunded mandate over $50 million on governments, which the Chair sustained before the House voted to proceed anyway, 274-141.

Rep. William Clay offered a motion to recommit that would have struck the exemption sections and added minimum wage provisions for the Northern Mariana Islands; it failed 181-243, with Democrats 180-28 in favor and Republicans 0-214 opposed.
The bill passed 282-143: Democrats 203-5 in favor, Republicans 78-137 against.

Per the rule, the text of H.R. 3846 as passed was added to the end of H.R. 3081, and H.R. 3846 itself was laid on the table; no further action on it appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed the higher wage and the industries that won exemptions came out ahead, because no raise ever took effect and the federal minimum wage stayed at $5.15. Low-wage workers gained nothing from the two years of work this bill received.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and exempt industries; low-wage workers got nothing

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: They would owe up to $1.00 more per hour for their lowest-paid staff — the direct cost of the raise — unless their state opts out and keeps $5.15.

The bill broadens the overtime exemption for computer professionals to cover network, database, and internet-related work at $27.63 an hour or more, so more tech workers lose overtime pay rights — a benefit to employers at those workers' expense.
A new exemption would remove minimum wage and overtime protections from sales employees who meet compensation thresholds, cutting labor costs for companies that rely on commissioned sales staff.
Licensed funeral directors and embalmers would be fully exempt from minimum wage and overtime requirements, a direct cost saving for funeral homes paid for by those workers' pay protections.
States gain the power to set their own wage floor as low as $5.15 in place of the federal rate — flexibility for states, but a pathway that can leave a state's lowest-paid workers without the raise.
